Replay

Authoring a feature in Godot

4 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
One-time setupThe accepted first milestoneReferences and shared extractionCreate a draftCommands and boundaries

Replay Scrapyard now has an optional Replay editor dock and an F6 ability workbench. The first complete example is Salvefield: a placed zone with radius, duration, pulse timing and a referenced healing status. Its existing rules and stock balance are preserved; drafts exercise additions without entering the canonical catalog until reviewed.

One-time setup#

Build/import the project normally. replay_authoring.json opts into installation of the Replay Authoring addon, enabled in this project's project.godot. The worker needs Python plus the Odin development toolchain; Nix is a fallback when Odin is not on PATH. The editor shows job progress while remaining responsive. Native authoring/testing jobs target macOS/Linux; they are development tools, not browser gameplay services.

The accepted first milestone#

  1. Open data/abilities/salvefield.tres in the Inspector. status is now a StatusDef Resource picker. Choose a status by Resource instead of remembering its numeric ID. The bake validates type/path/membership and stores the stable ID.
  2. Change radius, duration or pulse timing. Save & Validate Content checks the typed definitions, cross-references and registered enemy view scenes. Deliberately set radius to -1: the dock reports the exact Resource/field, and activating the issue opens it. Correct the value and validate again.
  3. Open dev/ability_workbench.tscn and press F6. Refresh authored data reloads saved data into the isolated preview. State, progress, playback speed and spatial guides make the configured area easy to inspect. Invalid refresh keeps the prior validated display. Enemy previews provide the corresponding hurt/death/charge behavior and pause their child animation too.
  4. Run isolated encounter explicitly admits a copied ability definition into a new development game. The workbench equips it through a normal Profile action, starts through Ready/Start, hurts the player through an admitted development action and casts through the normal ability action. It does not edit live World.
  5. Export reproduction writes user://workbench.rplrec. Verify last reproduction invokes the existing offline recording verifier. Return to preview closes the encounter and restores its temporary environment settings.
  6. Replay rejected prediction runs the authored ability with a predicted cast that is later corrected away, compares against an uninterrupted reference and audits frames/events. Test checkpoint takeover captures a mid-ability checkpoint, restores a new epoch and compares continuation. Results include casts/health, checkpoint/final ticks and a canonical hash.
  7. Run network encounter launches a real host/client pair at 0, 80 or 150 ms. Both equip the selected definition, the host casts, and they must agree on a retained public world hash. Jobs have deadlines, cancellation and preserved logs.
  8. Back in the editor, Save & Bake Content publishes the canonical artifact through the same extractor. The dock shows current/stale status. Save other independently edited Resources first; the buttons save open scenes and the selected saved Resource. Failed validation/baking preserves the last valid files.

The milestone was exercised through the actual editor plugin and running workbench, not only through equivalent CLI commands. Acceptance evidence records the exact checks and limits.

References and shared extraction#

Ability status, mob boom_status, and combo present/incoming/output now reference StatusDef Resources. Optional missing references bake to ID 0. Required ones fail validation. Referenced statuses must be catalog resources under data/status; duplicate/missing IDs and invalid values are rejected.

defs/bake_gun, bake_mob, bake_status, bake_combo and bake_ability contain one explicit mapping each. Catalog admission, export, validation, preview and isolated authoring scenarios reuse them. Inspector hints do not define game rules. The old catalog's canonical bytes are unchanged by this migration.

Runner appearances are now an Inspector array of ScrapRunnerStyle Resources, with stable look IDs and idle/run textures. Swapping or reorganizing styles needs no Becca/Joe/unknown fields in the view script. The three existing gameplay look IDs/capacity remain an explicit game contract; duplicate/missing styles reject.

Create a draft#

Choose a source definition, a kind and a lower-case name in the Replay dock, then Create Feature Draft. It creates scripts/drafts/NAME as one staged directory, refuses overwrites/traversal names, and reserves an explicit available stable ID under a lock. Existing IDs are never regenerated from filename order.

An ability draft contains a duplicated definition, preview scene, isolated workbench scene, metadata, README and scenario entry point. An actor draft contains its definition, composed visual script/scene, registration, authored preview and scenario entry point. It inherits the existing enemy root binding and gives the new visual component detached display data. New gameplay rules/state and specific feature assertions are marked TODO; no authority or migration policy is invented. The worker builds and previews a new draft before reporting success.

Drafts remain outside data/archetypes discovery. To adopt one, review its rules and compatibility, move its definition into the appropriate data directory using Godot's FileSystem tools, update references, add actor registration when applicable, then validate/bake and add feature-specific assertions. The generic scenario is a starting check, not evidence for rules that have not been implemented.

Commands and boundaries#

tools/authoring.py backs every editor/workbench command and writes structured results/logs under .godot/replay_authoring/jobs. Use it from CI with explicit --project, --framework, --godot, --result and the action. Direct catalog checks remain python3 tools/stock.py --check; rebaking requires Godot and a current compiled extractor.

The tooling preserves the last valid preview/artifact on rejected edits, keeps live content admission explicit, and never sends messages to external services. It adds startup validation and development processes; it makes no frame-time improvement claim. Kit and the original sibling Scrapyard remain independently runnable, with their source unchanged.
